title: The spirit-touched
summary: People who brush against spirits without fully Awakening.

claims.text: Many people begin by hearing dead relatives, meeting grown-up versions of childhood imaginary friends or seeing visions; untrained, such gifts usually worsen.
Most of the spirit-touched never learn to control what they sense, even with help, and some Dreamspeakers work as counsellors to aid them.
A would-be Dreamspeaker taught by spirits instead of a human mentor often arrives with odd notions about the Tradition.

title: Baruti
summary: The Storytellers, wandering keepers of lost tales.

claims.text: Baruti tell that in an age before the Gauntlet, wanderers worked magic and kept old tales, and a few survived the great change.
Their early aim of keeping the Age of Sorrows remembered widened into saving the tales of every lost people and vanished place.
Once the settled world gave up shamanism, Baruti in its realms became troubadours, messengers and wandering holy folk.

title: Independent Dreamspeakers
summary: Shamans Awakened by spirits rather than teachers.

claims.text: Other Traditions expect mad spirit-Awakened mages to turn Marauder, but Awakening often cures the madness or at least stops it from getting worse.
Unlike Orphans, Independents all drift to the Dreamspeakers in time, pushed by their spirit mentors or found by the Tradition.
When farming and cities arose, most shamans withdrew to the wilds, but a few learned the spirits of towns, fields and human works.
Skilled at striking bargains with spirits, they grew just as skilled at bargaining with and fooling Sleepers.
By the Hellenistic and T'ang eras they had spread across the Old World as fortune tellers and con artists; rivals call them Wheelers or Thieves.

title: Keepers of the Sacred Flame
summary: Shamans who save the ways of conquered peoples.

claims.text: The Keepers hold that shamans of defeated peoples can keep some traditions alive while living with the loss.
Some spirits suggest the practice is older than modern humans, reaching back to Neanderthal magic.
One strand traces to the first century, when a Pompeii merchant and linear spirit-worker named Flavius Longinus Didacus lived through the eruption.

title: Red Spear Society
summary: The Spirit Warriors at the heart of the Dreamspeakers.

claims.text: Insofar as the Dreamspeakers form one Tradition at all, it is mostly through the Red Spears.
Walking Hawk, a Seneca shaman, followed a vision to the Convocation and travelled far to bring other spirit masters together.
Walking Hawk's followers took the name Brotherhood of the Unseen Face, collecting the world's masks and totems to show the truth beneath them.
Withdrawal is as old as society itself and appears in the earliest accounts of shamans and in cave art.
It grows common both in hard times and in times of plenty, since well-fed people seek less guidance and frustrated shamans may leave.
Shamanism is practised for a tribe or community rather than for oneself, and frustration at a tribe that will not listen is a common reason to leave.

title: Walking between the worlds
summary: The Dreamspeaker view of magic and the Umbra.

claims.text: Dreamspeakers can work magic because they live in the material realm and the Umbra at once and can act in each.
The spirit lands are also lands of the dead; the shades who keep ties to the living dwell in the Dark Umbra.
Becoming a shaman always involves a symbolic death and rebirth into both realms, and cutting oneself off from either world brings harm.
